headline_marked: [[Tesla to sell Cybercabs]] to customers by year-end, despite federal safety investigation
headline: Tesla to sell Cybercabs to customers by year-end, despite federal safety investigation
summary: The autonomous two-seater lacks traditional controls and faces a federal safety investigation, which could impact its legal operation.
details: Tesla announced it will start selling its autonomous Cybercab to customers by the end of 2024. This two-seater vehicle is designed without a steering wheel or other traditional manual controls.

Initially, all Cybercabs produced are for Tesla's own robotaxi fleet. The company plans to gradually deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to third-party customers, starting small and scaling up.

This move follows earlier hints about selling robotaxis and represents a shift from CEO Elon Musk's long-standing plan to enable privately owned Teslas to become self-driving taxis via software updates. That original plan has not yet materialized.

Currently, Tesla owners can subscribe to Full Self-Driving (Supervised), which still requires human oversight. A fully unsupervised version of FSD is now projected for release to customers in the second quarter of next year, another delay for existing owners.

If both timelines hold, third-party fleet customers could potentially operate Cybercab robotaxi services before current Tesla owners gain access to unsupervised autonomous capabilities in their personal vehicles.

Musk emphasized that the Cybercab is primarily intended as a "transport as a service" vehicle, not a car for personal ownership. He expects the vast majority of Cybercabs to be Tesla-owned and operated.

A significant hurdle for Tesla's Cybercab plans is an ongoing investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). The federal regulator is probing whether the vehicle meets safety standards.

Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) currently mandate manual controls like brake pedals. NHTSA is examining Tesla's self-certification process and the technical data behind it, with the investigation's outcome potentially affecting the Cybercab's legal operation.

headline_marked: [[Flapping Airplanes raises $1B Series A]] at a $6B valuation, quadrupling its worth in 9 months
headline: Flapping Airplanes raises $1B Series A at a $6B valuation, quadrupling its worth in 9 months
summary: The year-old AI lab, co-led by Index and Lux, secured the massive round just nine months after a $180M seed round, boosting its valuation from $1.5B to $6B.
details: Year-old startup Flapping Airplanes has announced a $1 billion Series A funding round, co-led by Index and Lux, reportedly at a $6 billion valuation. The company aims to train large AI models with significantly less data.

This substantial investment comes just nine months after the company launched with a $180 million seed round. That initial round had valued the company at $1.5 billion, meaning its valuation has quadrupled in less than a year.

Earlier backers Sequoia, GV, and Kleiner Perkins also participated in the new round. Additional investors include Valor, Atreides, A*, and Nvidia, highlighting broad confidence in the startup's vision.

Flapping Airplanes was founded by Aidan Smith, a former Neuralink team member and Thiel fellow, and brothers Asher and Ben Spector. Asher holds a statistics PhD from Stanford, while Ben, a computer science PhD student from Stanford, also founded the influential Prod accelerator.

Prod, a five-year-old student-run startup accelerator, has been described as "one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley." Sequoia partner David Cahn, an investor, characterized Flapping Airplanes' founders as building the "young person's AGI lab."

The founders describe their core technology as "the world's most complete megakernel framework." This framework can perform entire training runs, serve inference, play video games, and even do all three simultaneously within a single kernel.

They claim their framework can "overlap memory-bound inference with compute-bound training," optimizing GPU usage by running different task types concurrently. This approach aims to maximize chip efficiency, suggesting AI has much more potential to unlock from current hardware.

The ultimate goal is to create intelligent systems that are significantly cheaper to train and run, without needing to ingest vast amounts of internet data. With this fresh $1 billion, Flapping Airplanes plans to expand its team and accelerate its mission to achieve data-efficient AI.
